newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - Delta Air chairman to retire.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Delta Air chairman to retire.

text.p: Delta Air Lines Inc's announcement that Ronald Allen will step down as the head of the nation's third largest airline took industry experts by surprise Monday, with some suggesting his resignation followed a rift with the board about the airline's strategic focus.

Although Allen is credited with returning Delta to profitability following losses in the early 1990s, some analysts said his successor will likely wield a sharper cost-cutting knife and will dampen the pilots union's new bid for wage increases.
Allen's departure after 34 years with Delta surprised Wall Street analysts and Delta employees.
"Certainly his departure seems abrupt. And perhaps not entirely voluntary, but that's just speculation," said Samuel Buttrick, an airline analyst with PaineWebber.
Allen's retirement, set for July 31, sparked rumors on Wall Street that his departure would allow Delta to renew merger talks with Continental Airlines Inc.
The two carriers held merger discussions last fall. Allen had opposed a combination with Delta and those talks were quickly abandoned, analysts said.
While some industry experts speculated that Allen's departure would allow Delta's board to reopen merger talks, other experts said they doubted merger hopes played a role in Allen's retirement.
Continental officials could not be reached for comment.
Other scenarios included possibilities that Allen and the board may have disagreed on the airlines' strategic growth plans or possible management changes, analysts said.
"He's brought the company through a big restructuring, so surprised he's leaving now .... but I don't read anything sinister into this," said Jeffrey Long, an analyst with J.P. Morgan.
"This is a big surprise. One take could be that he wants to enjoy his life. It can be as simple as that," said Edward Starkman, an airline analyst with Dillon Read.

Allen, 55, joined Delta part-time in 1963. He was named president and chief operating officer in 1983, then chairman and chief executive officer in 1987. He became president in 1990 and resumed that title in 1993.
Allen will retire when his contract expires July 31. He will stay on as a consultant and advisory director.

Delta said a search committee would be formed and Allen will work with the board to find a successor. Delta will meet with Wall Street analysts on Tuesday, but is not likely to elaborate on its plans to tap a successor, analysts said.
"They will cast a wide net. They are as likely to look inside the industry as outside," Starkman said.

"There is the chance that the successor will be more attentive to competitive pressures within the industry and will pay more attention to costs," said Joseph Blasi, a professor at Rutgers University's School of Management and Labor Relations.

Delta's pilots union said Allen's departure was "totally unexpected." The pilots' master executive council met with Allen on Monday, asking to reopen negotiations on a four-year contract its members ratified only one year ago.

Delta's pilots ratified a four-year contract in April 1996. Its provisions included a 2 percent pay cut in return for stock options, a profit-sharing plan comparable to those enjoyed by other Delta employees, a seat on the Atlanta-based company's board and improved retirement benefits.

Delta's pilots now contend that Delta's financial situation has improved. Delta awarded pay increases to its non-union employees, and pilots at carriers such as AMR Corp's American Airlines and UAL Corp's United Airlines recently secured pay increases.
"Recent events at both our company and in our industry raise serious questions about the fairness and equity of maintaining the status quo," the Delta pilots union said.
Delta's pilots said they wil pursue the wage increase regardless of the management change.
